I largely agree about the danger, but as I was reading this, I couldn't help thinking about the staggering contradiction. At the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics on July 26, 2024, a beheaded Marie-Antoinette appeared to the music of Gojira (a band I actually really like), accompanied by the revolutionary refrain “Ah! Ça ira, ça ira, ça ira, les aristocrates on les pendra” (“The aristocrats, we will hang them”). People all over the world watched the performance. The French Republic has a bloody history, and whatever the more radical ambitions of some May ’68 thinkers, violence has an undeniable place in its political tradition. It just does. Which is why far-left groups that glorify “revolutionary violence” consider themselves heirs to that very heritage, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon is pretty open about his attachment to it as well. So simply insisting that violence has no place in French political battles, in my opinion, misses a much deeper political problem. The question is what that violence seeks to accomplish and against whom. Condemning it is certainly necessary to preserve the state's monopoly on legitimate force and maintain some degree of social cohesion. But without understanding the resentment directed at the Republic itself, such condemnations tell us very little about the political forces driving it.

Some time ago, I came across research from ETH Zürich showing that 27% of 108,667 large Ethereum swaps were executed at suboptimal prices.

Researchers analyzed swaps over $30K and found that better routing could have saved nearly 30,000 trades at least $30.

Here are 5 things I learned ↓

1️⃣ A direct swap doesn't always give you the most tokens

Let's say you're swapping $ETH for $USDC.

You have several options:

• Swap directly through an ETH/USDC pool
• Route through ETH → USDT → USDC
• Split your order across several liquidity pools

Each option has different liquidity, price impact, and gas costs.

The ETH Zürich study found that optimizable trades could have received an average of 0.15% more through better routing.

For a $100,000 swap, that's an extra $150. This is exactly why DEX routers exist.

Fynd, for example, is the router @PropellerSwap built to find the best swap routes across liquidity pools.

But finding the best route is only half the problem.

2️⃣ Your swap route can become outdated before it executes

Here's something most DeFi users don't realize.

When you request a swap, the router calculates a route based on current liquidity and prices. You approve the tx, sign it, and wait for it to execute onchain.

That process can take a fraction of a second or stretch into tens of seconds.

During that time:

• Another trader can move prices in your chosen pool
• Liquidity providers can withdraw funds
• Arbitrageurs can eliminate price differences
• Market makers can update their quotes

So the route that looked optimal when you signed might be significantly worse when your transaction actually executes.

A perfectly calculated quote can become outdated within milliseconds.

3️⃣ Integrated route optimization

This was the most interesting part of my research.

Most traditional routers calculate execution paths before transactions are submitted, and some prepare alternative routes or fallback options in case conditions change.

These approaches still have limitations, and newer alternatives are emerging:

Fynd InBlock is one of them. Instead of relying on routes calculated beforehand, it lets block builders run an entirely new route search immediately before the tx executes.

• You submit a swap with an initial route
• The block builder processes preceding transactions
• Fynd, running inside the block builder, searches for a better route using the updated pool states
• If a better route exists, it can replace the original

It's essentially performing a fresh search based on the liquidity available at your exact position inside the block.

4️⃣ What if there's no optimal route?

Imagine swapping $50,000 in $ETH for $USDC.

Your original route uses Pool A, but another trader moves its price before your transaction executes.

Pool B now offers a better deal.

Instead of sticking with the outdated route, Fynd InBlock can discover Pool B and switch before execution.

If no better route exists, your trade uses the original route, subject to the same minimum output requirement.

5️⃣ Beyond DEX aggregators

Better execution benefits the entire trading infrastructure:

• Wallets can offer more reliable swaps
• Trading terminals can reduce failed transactions and slippage
• Aggregators can compete on actual execution quality
• Block builders can earn revenue from improving routes

The ETH Zürich research showed how much value inefficient routing leaves on the table.

My prediction is that the next moat in DEX execution isn't finding the best route faster, but rather finding the best route at the exact moment your trade executes.

If you want to read more about how Fynd InBlock works, start here:
https://t.co/aZcClI5kuh

⚒️ DAILY METALS PULSE — October 26, 2026

A steadier start to the week. Gold and silver recovered as oil eased, giving markets some breathing room ahead of Wednesday’s Fed decision. Encouraging, but one green session doesn’t establish a trend.

⚛️ URANIUM
The longer-term picture keeps strengthening. Cameco’s latest monthly benchmark puts long-term uranium at $96.50/lb for September, up from $86.50 at year-end. Meanwhile, Britain’s push to accelerate reactor approvals reinforces the direction of travel: more nuclear capacity—and future fuel requirements. Proposed reactors still need to become operating plants, but the demand pipeline keeps developing.

🥈 SILVER
Front-month futures settled around $54.11/oz, up 0.7%. A welcome recovery after last week’s pressure. I’m watching whether silver can build on this as investors weigh interest rates against the outlook for industrial demand.

🔶 COPPER
Latest indicative pricing was around $6.51/lb, up roughly 0.6%. This week’s major tech earnings could influence expectations for spending on data centres and power infrastructure. Copper remains closely tied to that investment, while tariff uncertainty adds volatility.

🥇 GOLD
December futures settled at $4,038.40/oz, up 0.8%. Lower oil helped ease inflation concerns, but the Fed’s tone could decide whether this rebound gains traction.

👀 MY TAKE
A constructive session, with a demanding week still ahead. I’m watching oil, yields and the dollar for the next move in precious metals—and utility contracting for uranium.
My strongest conviction remains uranium’s long-term fuel-demand story. Equity volatility can test patience; the pace of contracting and new mine supply will test the thesis.

Anthropic is now generating ~$2 of revenue for every $1 of compute spend - up from just $0.40 a year ago.

This is a 5x improvement in compute efficiency and clear evidence that AI demand is being monetised at the model layer.

But it doesn’t automatically solve the ROI question for the infrastructure stack. Model companies are customers of the compute; hyperscalers and neoclouds are the ones that have to earn a return on the GPUs, power and data centers after depreciation and financing costs.

The market is currently focused on the cash-flow gap and higher cost of capital. The efficiency gains and sold-out capacity suggest the longer-term demand thesis is still intact.

We continue to see selective opportunities in the highest-quality AI enablers. https://t.co/YKr5pL78cE

@Forbes just named me one of America's greatest living optimists. #76! It was a huge honor.

After all, while pessimists might be “right” for the time being, optimists do everything that drives progress.

All the great successes I know are huge optimists.

Supporting optimism is my life.

Free email sounded crazy to pessimists. But Hotmail was built by optimists, Sabeer Bhatia and Jack Smith.

Free phone calls and video calls sounded even crazier to pessimists. But Skype was born by optimists, Niklas Zennstrom and Janus Fries.

An electric car company and a private space company? Crazier still to a pessimist, but Tesla and SpaceX were built by the biggest optimist anywhere, Elon Musk.

Satoshi Nakamoto is an optimist, willing to transform the entire global economy with a trusted 3rd party in software around Bitcoin.

Every one of those started with an entrepreneur painting a picture of a world nobody had seen yet. My job was just to believe in the world they were creating, and to say yes to them and encourage them forward.

So the award really belongs to the founders. They supply the optimism. I just keep buying it.

After over 30 years of trading, here is what I've learned.

First, my Duke MBA is +/- worthless for trading, but does help me understand jargon and fundamentals, so not a total waste.

Second, it is like poker. The key is folding most of the time and only betting when your turn comes around.

Third, most years, it's only 2-4 / year that you should place trades/allocate capital. This is the key. You do NOT buy and sell and every week, every day or even every month.

Fourth, and this more art than science, you just wait for some narrative to get so ridiculous in one direction that you have to wade in for the reverse.

Examples this year, which I posted on as times to buy. Let me repeat this again, everything I mentioned below as a time to buy is recorded on my X feed.

Third, I said to buy bonds a month ago when the the 10 year was at 5.3%.

A week or so ago, I said to buy semis, buy the SOXX. I also think buying Brazil, EWZ, is the play now.

Those two last picks above might look stupid a week or two from now. But just wait. 

In 5-6 months, I will repost this with the SOXX and EWZ performance since this post. My guess, a 30-50% gain easy.

Stop with the one-day options, the leverage, the 3x ETFs and all the bullshit.

Stop with being smart and analyzing all the trends and looking perfect.

Buy low. Then buy lower, then buy higher, but only of the things that almost must come back. 

You will kill every hedgie on the street. I do.

• ~40 million customers sit below the $100K tier
